title: Doubts, Rejection, and an Offer of Rest
overview: From prison, John the Baptist asks whether Jesus really is the one they were waiting for; Jesus answers, honors John, warns the towns that ignored him, and invites the weary to come to him.

parts.label: John's question from prison (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: John, jailed by the ruler Herod Antipas, sends followers to ask if Jesus is the promised Messiah, perhaps because Jesus was not the conquering figure many expected. Jesus points to his deeds, which echo the prophet Isaiah's pictures of what God's coming rescue would look like.

parts.label: Jesus honors John (vv. 7-15)
parts.note: John was no reed bending in the wind and no pampered courtier; Jesus calls him the messenger promised by the prophet Malachi and the 'Elijah' expected to return before God acted. Verse 12 is famously hard, and scholars are unsure whether it means God's kingdom is under attack, as John's arrest suggests, or that eager people are forcing their way in.

parts.label: Children who won't play (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: Jesus pictures children in a square who sulk whether others play wedding music or funeral songs. People dismissed John as too strict and Jesus as too fond of feasting with outcasts, but Jesus says the outcome of each way of life will show who was right.

parts.label: Warnings to Galilean towns (vv. 20-24)
parts.note: Jesus says Tyre and Sidon, foreign cities condemned by earlier prophets, would have repented in sackcloth and ashes, rough clothing and ash worn to show grief, had they seen what Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum saw. He adds that even Sodom would still be standing, so judgment will be harder on these towns, a severe warning the text does not soften.

parts.label: Hidden from the wise (vv. 25-27)
parts.note: Jesus thanks God that people proud of their learning missed what ordinary, childlike people understood. He then claims a unique, two-way knowing between himself and the Father, which Christians read as a claim to share God's own identity.

parts.label: An easy yoke (vv. 28-30)
parts.note: A yoke was the wooden frame on working animals, and teachers of the day spoke of their teaching as a yoke people took on. Jesus offers his way as light and himself as gentle to people worn down by life and by heavy demands.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether John himself was truly doubting Jesus or sent the question mainly so his own followers would hear the answer.
think: When something you hoped for turns out different from what you expected, what kind of evidence actually helps you decide whether it is still the real thing?
